title: Tricky lists for max
idea: TOOL: reason about ties, negatives, and single-item lists for the max pattern.

exercises.explanation: Among negatives, -3 is closest to zero, so it is the biggest. Starting best at the first value handles this correctly.

exercises.prompt: Why can starting best at 0 give a WRONG answer for [-10, -3, -8]?
options: No negative beats 0, so best would stay 0 — a value not in the list
exercises.explanation: 0 is bigger than every negative, so best never updates and reports 0 — which isn't even in the list. Start at nums[0].
All equal, so best stays at the first value, 5. The max of all-equal values is that value.
best starts at 42 and nothing else exists to beat it. One item means that item is the max.

exercises.prompt: With ties for biggest (e.g. two 9s), the max loop still reports a single value, 9.
exercises.explanation: Max reports the biggest VALUE, not how many times it appears. Two 9s still give a max of 9.

exercises.prompt: In [3, -2, 7, -9, 7], what does best hold at the end?
exercises.explanation: best rises to 7 and the second 7 ties (no change). Mixed signs are fine because best started at a real value.

exercises.prompt: Which lists have a biggest value of exactly 0? (pick all)
exercises.explanation: The first three top out at 0. The last has a 1, so its biggest is 1.

exercises.prompt: A list of golf scores can go below par (negative). Why does the best-so-far start matter here?
options: Starting at the first real score, not 0, lets negative scores win correctly
exercises.explanation: Real data like golf scores can be negative. Starting best at a real value avoids the 'stuck at 0' bug.

exercises.prompt: If you are not sure your max works on negatives, a quick fix is to test it on an all-negative list.
exercises.explanation: An all-negative list is the classic case that exposes the 'start at 0' bug. Testing it builds confidence.
100 is the top value; the 99 never beats it. Repeats of the max don't change the answer.
